## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.50065.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.50065.sa1)

In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

Your paper establishes the molecular mechanism used to determine and maintain terminal identity of cholinergic motor neurons in C. elegans. Your demonstration of the dual function of UNC-3 (Collier/Ebf) in directly promoting identity features of cholinergic motor neurons and in preventing terminal features of other ventral cord neuron types is striking. The role of the Hox protein LIN-39 that interacts with UNC-3 explains this dual role. Your data therefore shows that UNC-3 and LIN-39 co-activate terminal identity features of cholinergic motor neurons.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "A terminal selector prevents a Hox transcriptional switch to safeguard motor neuron identity throughout life" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Marianne Bronner as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

The general opinion of the reviewers is that the paper represents an important contribution to the field and presents concepts that should be of general interest to those studying neural specification in general and production of neurotransmitters in particular. However, while the regulatory network is clearly presented in the paper, there are some significant questions that remain and need to be addressed before the paper can be considered for publication.

In particular, a technical problem appears to be in the ChIP-PCR that you performed. It seems that are available ChIP-seq data that would be more valuable if they are of quality. If not, you should sequence your ChIP with Lin-39 and redo them in a unc-3 mutant. This should also complemented by a detailed description of the unc-3 phenotype, as suggested by reviewer #2.

The other significant issue resides with the biochemistry in order to elucidate how these proteins interact with the promoters to regulate cell fate and neurotransmitters. The interaction between Lin39 and Unc-3 should be clarified.

Furthermore, the paper would gain by being presented in a simpler way so it would reach a wider audience. We also ask that you remove unsupported claims, as described by the reviewers below.

Reviewer #1:

The manuscript by Feng et al. examines mechanisms through which UNC-3 transcription factor induces expression of genes expressed in cholinergic motor neurons while at the same time it suppresses expression of VD GABAergic motor neuron markers. The study provides a detailed genetic dissection of this problem, concluding that derepression of VD identity in the absence of UNC-3 is dependent on LIN-39 transcription factor. Interestingly, UNC-3 does not repress LIN-39 transcriptionally, instead it diverts its activity from VD target genes to cholinergic VNC motor neuron identity genes. The authors then investigate whether LIN-39 is sequestered away from VD enhancers by UNC-3 to regulatory elements associated with cholinergic motor neuron genes, as has been suggested for many other transcription factors (e.g. Mef2D-Crx interactions in retina (Andzelm et al., 2015) or Isl1-Lhx3/Onecut1 interaction in mammalian motor neurons (Rhee et al., 2016)). However, biochemical tests do not support this model. The authors do not detect physical interaction between UNC-3 and LIN-39, and they suggest that LIN-39 in not a limiting factor as it is not displaced from its binding sites in the absence of UNC-3. At the same time, they contradict this conclusion by demonstrating that VD genes can be induced in the context of cholinergic motor neurons by simply increasing the dosage of LIN-39.

While the genetic analysis and characterization of mutant phenotypes is rigorous and convincing, I am less convinced by the chromatin immunoprecipitation data. Mainly, their ChIP-PCR analysis lacks proper negative controls (regions not bound by transcription factors). More importantly, ChIP-PCR is an inferior method for the analysis of transcription factor binding, prone to false positives and general misinterpretation of transcription factor binding data. Surprisingly, the authors take minimal advantage of the existing LIN-39 ChIP-seq data. If they believe the data are of good quality, they should rely on them to demonstrate binding to the discovered enhancers. If they believe that their data are better, they should sequence their material and include it in the manuscript. In addition, they should perform ChIP-seq analysis in unc-3 animals to substantiate their claim that LIN-39 does not relocate from cholinergic enhancers to VD enhancers.

Overall, the manuscript is long and dense. The authors should make an attempt to streamline it and simplify it by focusing on the most important points.

In several places the authors state that a "uniform" population of cholinergic motor neurons gives rise to distinct VC and VD neuronal identities in unc-3 animals. However, VNC cholinergic neurons are not a uniform population as they are composed of five different subtypes. Furthermore, the data clearly show that VC neurons are mainly derived from AS neurons while VD neurons are primarily derived from DA/B and VA/B neurons.

It appears that all tested sites listed in Supplementary file 2 show LIN-39 binding – this raises the concern that the ChIP is globally enriched for DNA and any tested regions will be positive. It is essential to include negative genomic regions in ChIP-PCR experiments and in general it would be preferable to perform ChIP-seq analysis. The authors should show existing LIN-39 ChIP-seq tracks for each of the examined regulatory regions.

The authors conclude that LIN-39 is not a limiting factor. How do they interpret the LIN-39 overexpression results that leads to the activation of VD markers in VNC cholinergic neurons?

The authors should provide better description of LIN-39 expression pattern and describe its mutant phenotype in detail.

The authors present their model as revealing completely new mechanisms of regulation of gene expression. However, cell type-specific transcription factor binding to distinct enhancers is a well-known phenomenon with several publications detailing how interactions with different transcription factors result in relocation of TF complexes from one region to another. The authors should present their work in the context of this literature.

Reviewer #2:

This work from the Kratsios lab aims to understand how neurons acquire and importantly maintain their fate. It takes advantage of the well-studied and characterized C. elegans nervous system, focusing on motor neurons. The wealth of genetic, cellular and molecular tools makes C. elegans an appropriate model system. Additionally, motor neurons are particularly interesting cell type because they acquire and maintain a generic motor neuron fate, plus an appropriate motor neuron subtype. Thus, the topic is relevant and addressed with appropriate tools.

Previous work, with a significant contribution by Kratsios, established that the motor neuron terminal selector unc-3 directly activates and maintains a sub-set of motor neuron fates. These findings are confirmed and expanded in this manuscript. Of note, the degron experiment presented here is a nice confirmation of this hypothesis. Similar to other species, Hox genes coordinate their activity to establish distinct motor neurons fates. In this work, lin-39 recovered though a screen and mab-5 as candidate Hox genes regulating terminal genes. Again, there is a nice confirmation of this lin-39 as terminal selector hypothesis by ChIP and the Lin-39 degron allele.

One interesting take home from this work is the underlying gene regulatory network. Not all motor neurons acquire the same "default state" upon unc-3 removal and divide themselves into 3 groups based on the set of analyzed makers: VD, VC or undetermined. These results suggest a heterogeneous underlying regulatory network controlling motor neuron fate that might be canalized by unc-3 activity. Because it is at the crux of the phenotype, the author should be very clear describing the phenotype. Is this an expressivity issue or it is 100% penetrant with high expressivity in always the same cells across animals? or is not fully penetrant or with variable expressivity across motor neurons? Depending on the phenotype, combining all motor neurons in a single group might not be the appropriate data representation. Additionally, it will significantly change the conclusions that can be derived from the data.

At large, this work revolves around the combinatorial control of cell fate. It further dissects the unc-3/Hox dependent regulation of motor neuron fate. Activation of neuronal type-specific features and preventing the expression of different cell fates is a well-described transcription factor activity during chick and mouse motor neuron development. I am confused by the strong emphasis on "transcriptional switch". It is stressed as a novel insight but there is not tangible mechanistic evidence for it. Moreover, the phenotypes are changes in gene expression with repression and activation of terminal genes, not a complete switch of fates as far as I can tell. At the mechanistic level of gene regulation by transcription factors, there is no evidence of unc-3 or lin-39 switching binding targets or DNA motif preference. Additionally, transcription factor target switch by changing binding partners has been extensively described, even during motor neuron development.

Finally, there is a trend to make claims that are not strictly supported by the data or a lack of precision describing phenotypes. In my opinion, this work has a few confirmatory results, the significant claim is not supported by the data and thus it does not provide a significant conceptual nor technical leap for eLife.

Reviewer #3:

This paper investigated the molecular mechanism used to determine and maintain terminal identity features of cholinergic motor neurons in the C. elegans ventral nerve cord. The authors showed dual function of the terminal selector UNC-3 (Collier/Ebf) in directly promoting identity features of cholinergic motor neurons and indirectly preventing expression of terminal features of three other ventral cord neuron types (VD, VC, CA). Through an unbiased genetic screen, the authors identified the Hox protein LIN-39 (Scr/Dfd/Hox4-5) to be required for ectopic expression of VD and VC features in unc-3 mutants. In summary, the data presented in the paper supports the dual role of UNC-3: UNC-3 and LIN-39 directly co-activate terminal identity features of cholinergic motor neurons; UNC-3 antagonizes the LIN-39's ability of activating terminal features of alternative neuronal identities.

The paper is well written. However, some points should be addressed or clarified.

- It has been previously shown that unc-3 and lin-39 in act synergistically to activate expression of cholinergic motor neuron terminal identity genes (Kratsios et al., 2017). This study identified a new role of unc-3 in antagonizing the LIN-39's function of activating terminal features of alternative neuronal identities. The authors should perform additional experiments to provide a mechanistic insight into how UNC-3 prevents LIN-39-mediated transcriptional switch for inducing expression of alternative identity features.

- The authors showed data to indicate that lin-39 and unc-30 act in parallel to co-activate VD terminal identity genes. However, the authors also showed that ectopic expression of VD markers is not dependent on UNC-30. The contradictory results should be discussed. Does the data suggest that lin-39 acts with yet-to-be identified factor(s) to activate ectopic expression of VD features in unc-3 mutants?

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claims.claim: 12.1 ± 2.6 (mean ± STDV) out of the 39 unc-3-depleted motor neurons in the ventral nerve cord ectopically express VD markers.
claims.source: Importantly, 12.1 ± 2.6 (mean ± STDV) out of the 39 unc-3-depleted MNs in the VNC were ectopically expressing these VD markers, suggesting that not all unc-3-depleted MNs acquire VD terminal identity features.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from the manuscript.

claims.claim: GABAergic and cholinergic motor neurons are generated in normal numbers in unc-3 animals.
claims.source: Given that GABAergic and cholinergic MNs are generated in normal numbers in unc-3 animals (Kratsios et al., 2012), the increase in the number of neurons expressing the VD markers cannot be attributed to early developmental defects affecting MN numbers.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Kratsios et al., 2012).

claims.claim: unc-3-depleted motor neurons that acquire VD-like features do not express genes involved in GABA biosynthesis or genes selectively expressed in GABAergic motor neurons.
claims.source: We next asked whether these ~12 MNs adopt additional VD terminal identity features, such as expression of genes involved in GABA biosynthesis (unc-25/GAD and unc-47/VGAT), or selectively expressed in GABAergic MNs (ttr-39, klp-4). However, this does not appear to be the case, arguing against a complete cell fate switch (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, panel A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, panel A.

claims.claim: In the absence of unc-3, approximately one-third of cholinergic motor neurons (~12 out of 39) in the mid-body ventral nerve cord region gain some terminal identity features normally reserved for VD neurons.
claims.source: We conclude that, in the absence of unc-3, cholinergic MNs not only lose their original terminal identity, but a third of them (~12 out of 39) in the mid-body VNC region also gain some terminal identity features normally reserved for the sex-shared VD neurons (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and inference from the results.

claims.claim: VC-specific terminal identity markers ida-1, srb-16, and glr-5 are ectopically expressed in unc-3-depleted motor neurons.
claims.source: To test whether UNC-3 also prevents expression of terminal identity features of sex-specific cholinergic MNs, we examined three VC-specific terminal markers (glr-5, srb-16, ida-1 in Figure 1B) in hermaphrodite nematodes lacking unc-3. Again, we observed region-specific effects with 100% penetrance in the same cells across multiple animals (Figure 2C–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, panel B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, panel B.

claims.claim: 10.5 ± 3.7 (mean ± STDV) of the 39 unc-3-depleted motor neurons located in the mid-body region of the ventral nerve cord ectopically express VC markers.
claims.source: All three markers were ectopically expressed in 10.5 ± 3.7 (mean ± STDV) of the 39 unc-3-depleted MNs located in the mid-body region of the VNC (Figure 2C–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claims.claim: unc-3-depleted motor neurons that acquire VC-like features do not express genes necessary for acetylcholine biosynthesis.
claims.source: If these ~11 MNs fully adopt the VC terminal identity, then they should also express genes necessary for acetylcholine biosynthesis since VC neurons are cholinergic. However, this is not the case as expression of unc-17/VAChT and cho-1/ChT is dramatically affected in unc-3-depleted MNs (Kratsios et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Kratsios et al., 2012).

claims.claim: The VD-like and VC-like neurons in unc-3 hermaphrodites represent two distinct populations.
claims.source: Are the VD-like and VC-like neurons in unc-3 hermaphrodites distinct populations? To test this, we generated unc-3 hermaphrodites that carry a green fluorescent reporter for VC terminal identity (ida-1::gfp) and a red reporter for VD identity (ser-2::rfp). We found no overlap of the two reporters, indicating that the VD-like and VC-like neurons represent two distinct populations (Figure 2E–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E-F demonstrating no co-localization of VD and VC markers.

claims.claim: Terminal identity markers normally expressed in both VD and VC neurons (flp-11, ilys-4, twk-46) display an additive effect in unc-3 mutants, being ectopically expressed in both VD-like and VC-like populations.
claims.source: Lastly, terminal identity markers normally expressed in both VD and VC neurons (flp-11, ilys-4, twk-46) display an additive effect in unc-3 mutants, as they are ectopically expressed in both VD-like and VC-like populations, further suggesting the presence of distinct unc-3 MN populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, panels D-E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, panels D-E.

claims.claim: Loss of unc-3 in males results in loss of several cholinergic motor neuron terminal identity features.
claims.source: To test whether the dual function of UNC-3 applies to both sexes, we extended our analysis to C. elegans males. First, we showed that loss of unc-3 in males resulted in loss of several cholinergic MN terminal identity features (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: In unc-3 mutant males, 11.9 ± 3.9 (mean ± STDV) out of the 39 unc-3-depleted motor neurons ectopically express VD-specific terminal identity markers.
claims.source: Second, we observed ectopic expression of VD-specific terminal identity markers (oig-1, ser-2) in 11.9 ± 3.9 (mean ± STDV) out of the 39 unc-3-depleted MNs, indicating the presence of 'VD-like' neurons in the male nerve cord (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: unc-3 loss in males leads to ectopic expression of terminal identity markers for male-specific CA neurons.
claims.source: Lastly, we asked whether unc-3 loss leads to ectopic expression of terminal identity markers (ida-1, srb-16, glr-5) for male-specific CA neurons. Indeed, we found this to be the case (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting the adoption of 'CA-like' features by a population of unc-3-depleted MNs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: UNC-3 is continuously required to prevent expression of VD and VC terminal identity features.
claims.source: Auxin administration at the L4 stage (last larval stage before adulthood) on unc-3::mNG::AID; eft-3::TIR1 animals resulted in a dramatic depletion of UNC-3 at day one adult animals (24 hr after auxin). UNC-3 depletion was accompanied by ectopic expression of VD and VC terminal identity features in nerve cord MNs, demonstrating a post-embryonic requirement for UNC-3 (Figure 3D–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from auxin-inducible degradation experiments shown in Figure 3D-E.

claims.claim: UNC-3 does not act as a direct repressor of VD or VC terminal identity genes through its cognate COE binding motif.
claims.source: While it is known that UNC-3 acts directly – through its cognate binding site (COE motif) – to activate expression of a large battery of cholinergic MN identity genes, we did not find any COE motifs in the cis-regulatory region of VD or VC terminal identity genes (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis of cis-regulatory regions reported in Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: UNC-3 does not prevent expression of VD terminal identity genes by repressing UNC-30/PITX expression.
claims.source: Since UNC-30 is not expressed in cholinergic MNs (Jin et al., 1994), we hypothesized that UNC-3 prevents expression of UNC-30/PITX, leading to inactivation of VD terminal identity genes. However, this is not the case because: (1) ectopic unc-30 expression is not observed in unc-3-depleted MNs, and (2) the ectopic expression of the VD marker (ser-2) in unc-3 mutants was not abolished in unc-3; unc-30 double mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous work (Jin et al., 1994).

claims.claim: The mid-body Hox protein LIN-39 (Scr/Dfd/Hox4-5) is necessary for ectopic expression of VD and VC features in unc-3 mutants.
claims.source: To identify such factor(s), we embarked on an unbiased genetic screen. For the screen, we chose a transgenic gfp reporter strain for flp-11, an FMRF-like neuropeptide-encoding gene expressed in both VD and VC neurons (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which is markedly affected by UNC-3 (Figure 4A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, panels D-E). We mutagenized unc-3 (n3435); flp-11::gfp animals with ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS) and visually screened ~4200 haploid genomes for mutants in which ectopic flp-11::gfp expression in unc-3-depleted MNs is suppressed. We isolated one mutant allele (kas1) (Figure 4A–B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from a forward genetic screen shown in Figure 4A-B.

claims.claim: The kas1 mutation is a point mutation on the splice acceptor site in the second intron of lin-39.
claims.source: Upon a literature survey for TF mutants that are vulvaless, we stumbled across the mid-body Hox gene lin-39 (ortholog of Dfd/Scr in flies and Hox4-5 in vertebrates) (Aboobaker and Blaxter, 2003; Clark et al., 1993), and hypothesized that the molecular lesion of kas1 may lie in the lin-39 locus. Indeed, Sanger sequencing uncovered a point mutation on the splice acceptor site (WT: AG > kas1: AA) in the second intron of lin-39 (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data and reference to Figure 4C showing the molecular lesion.

claims.claim: lin-39 is required for ectopic expression of VD-specific terminal identity genes ser-2 and oig-1 in unc-3-depleted motor neurons.
claims.source: Because flp-11 is expressed in both VD and VC neurons, we next tested whether lin-39 is required for ectopic expression of VD-specific (ser-2, oig-1) and VC-specific (ida-1) terminal identity genes in unc-3-depleted MNs. We found this to be the case by either generating unc-3 (n3435); lin-39 (n1760) double mutants (for VD markers) or by performing cholinergic MN-specific RNAi for lin-39 in unc-3 (n3435) animals (for VC marker) (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D from double mutant and RNAi experiments.

claims.claim: lin-39 is co-expressed with unc-3 in wild-type cholinergic motor neurons at the mid-body region of the ventral nerve cord.
claims.source: Interestingly, this finding contradicts our initial hypothesis of UNC-3 repressing an intermediary TF in order to prevent expression of VD and VC features because lin-39 is co-expressed with (not repressed by) unc-3 in wild-type cholinergic MNs at the mid-body region of the VNC (Figure 4E), as evident by our single-cell analysis of unc-3 and lin-39 reporters (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell co-localization analysis shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: 28 cholinergic motor neurons co-express unc-3 and lin-39.
claims.source: Of note, 28 cholinergic MNs co-express unc-3 and lin-39, which is in close agreement with the total number of VD-like (12.1 ± 2.6) and VC-like (10.5 ± 3.7) cells observed in unc-3 mutants (Figure 4E–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from co-localization analysis shown in Figure 4E-F.

claims.claim: lin-39 acts cell-autonomously in cholinergic motor neurons.
claims.source: Moreover, we found that lin-39 acts cell-autonomously as cholinergic MN-specific RNAi against lin-39 in unc-3 (n3435) animals resulted in a significant reduction of ectopic terminal identity marker (flp-11, ida-1) expression (Figure 4B–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from cell-specific RNAi experiments shown in Figure 4B-D.

claims.claim: LIN-39 and MAB-5 act synergistically with UNC-3 to control expression of cholinergic motor neuron terminal identity genes.
claims.source: Our previous findings suggested that LIN-39 and UNC-3, together with another mid-body Hox protein, MAB-5 (Antp/Hox6-8) (Salser et al., 1993), act synergistically to control expression of two cholinergic MN terminal identity genes (unc-129, ortholog of human BMP; del-1/Degenerin like sodium channel [ortholog of human SCNN1G]) (Kratsios et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Kratsios et al., 2017; Salser et al., 1993).

claims.claim: Loss of lin-39 results in a statistically significant decrease in expression of cholinergic motor neuron terminal identity genes acr-2, dbl-1, unc-77, and slo-2.
claims.source: To test the extent of this synergy, we examined in lin-39 and mab-5 null animals the expression of 4 additional cholinergic MN terminal identity genes known to be controlled by UNC-3 (acr-2/nicotinic acetylcholine receptor; dbl-1/DPP/BMP-like; unc-77/sodium channel [ortholog of human NALCN], slo-2/potassium sodium-activated channel [ortholog of human KCNT1]) (Kratsios et al., 2012). In all four cases, we found a statistically significant decrease in lin-39 mutants, and this effect was exacerbated in lin-39; mab-5 double mutants (Figure 5A–B)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A-B and citation to previous work (Kratsios et al., 2012).

claims.claim: LIN-39 directly binds to the cis-regulatory regions of cholinergic motor neuron terminal identity genes acr-2, unc-129, dbl-1, del-1, unc-77, and slo-2.
claims.source: We analyzed available ChIP-Seq data for LIN-39 from the modENCODE project (Boyle et al., 2014) and found evidence for direct LIN-39 binding in the cis-regulatory of all six cholinergic MN terminal identity genes (unc-129, del-1, acr-2, dbl-1, unc-77, slo-2) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1, with citation to the modENCODE project (Boyle et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Multiple consensus LIN-39 binding sites are located within the LIN-39 ChIP-Seq peaks in the cis-regulatory region of cholinergic motor neuron terminal identity genes.
claims.source: Moreover, we identified multiple consensus LIN-39 binding sites (previously defined as GATTGATG) (Boyle et al., 2014) located within the LIN-39 ChIP-Seq peaks in the cis-regulatory region of the aforementioned genes (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis reported in Supplementary file 2 and citation to previous work (Boyle et al., 2014).

claims.claim: In the absence of UNC-3, LIN-39 binding is decreased in the cis-regulatory region of cholinergic motor neuron terminal identity genes.
claims.source: If this hypothesis is correct, one would expect decreased LIN-39 binding in the cis-regulatory region of cholinergic MN terminal identity genes in unc-3 mutants. By performing ChIP-Seq for LIN-39 in unc-3 mutant animals, we indeed observed decreased LIN-39 binding in the cis-regulatory region of the aforementioned genes (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: LIN-39 is continuously required for ectopic activation of VD and VC terminal identity genes in unc-3 null animals.
claims.source: Next, we sought to determine whether LIN-39 is continuously required for the ectopic activation of VD and VC terminal features observed in unc-3 null animals. Indeed, auxin administration at L4 stage on unc-3(n3435); lin-39::mNG::3xFLAG::AID animals carrying either a VD (ser-2), VC (glr-5), or VD/VC (flp-11) marker resulted in a statistically significant suppression of the unc-3 phenotype when compared to control (treated with ethanol) (Figure 6D–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from auxin-inducible degradation experiments shown in Figure 6D-F.

claims.claim: LIN-39 is expressed in wild-type VD neurons at the mid-body region of the ventral nerve cord.
claims.source: To this end, we leveraged our endogenous lin-39 reporter (lin-39::mNG::3xFLAG::AID) to assess expression in wild-type VD neurons at the mid-body region of the VNC, and found this to be the case (Figure 7A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from the endogenous lin-39 reporter shown in Figure 7A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: LIN-39 is required to induce expression of VD terminal identity genes ser-2 and oig-1.
claims.source: Next, we found that LIN-39 is required to induce expression of VD terminal identity genes (ser-2, oig-1) (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: lin-39 and unc-30 act in parallel to activate VD terminal identity genes ser-2 and flp-11.
claims.source: To test for synergistic effects, we focused on ser-2 and flp-11, two VD-expressed terminal identity genes mildly affected in lin-39 or unc-30 single mutants. We generated lin-39; unc-30 double mutants and observed stronger effects than either single mutant (Figure 7B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, panel E). Such additive effects indicate that lin-39 and unc-30 act in parallel to activate VD terminal identity genes.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from double mutant analysis shown in Figure 7B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2, panel E.

claims.claim: Expression of DD-specific marker flp-13 and genes expressed in both DD and VD neurons (unc-25/GAD, unc-47/VGAT) is unaffected in lin-39 mutants.
claims.source: Importantly, expression of other UNC-30 targets in GABAergic MNs, such as flp-13 (DD-specific terminal identity marker) (Cinar et al., 2005; Shan et al., 2005; Yu et al., 2017) and genes expressed in both DD and VD neurons (unc-25/GAD, unc-47/VGAT), is unaffected in lin-39 mutants (Figure 7B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, panel F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2, panel F, with citations to previous work (Cinar et al., 2005; Shan et al., 2005; Yu et al., 2017).

claims.claim: LIN-39 is continuously required to maintain expression of the VD terminal identity gene ser-2.
claims.source: To test for a maintenance role in VD neurons, we administered auxin at various post-developmental stages (L3, L4, day one adult) on animals carrying the lin-39::mNG::3xFLAG::AID allele. We found that LIN-39 is continuously required to maintain expression of the VD terminal identity gene ser-2 (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from auxin-inducible degradation experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Loss of unc-30 does not lead to ectopic activation of cholinergic motor neuron terminal identity genes in GABAergic VD neurons.
claims.source: Since the absence of UNC-3 leads to ectopic activation of VD-specific genes (Figure 5D), we next considered the converse possibility: Does the absence of UNC-30/PITX lead to ectopic activation of cholinergic MN terminal identity genes in GABAergic VD neurons? However, this appears not to be the case as expression of 4 cholinergic MN markers (acr-2, slo-1, unc-129, del-1), normally co-activated by UNC-3 and LIN-39 (Figure 5A–B), is unaffected in unc-30 mutants (Figure 7D–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D-F.

claims.claim: LIN-39 acts directly to activate VD-specific gene oig-1 by recognizing its cognate binding site.
claims.source: A previous study identified a minimal 125 bp cis-regulatory element (contained within the LIN-39 peak boundaries) upstream of oig-1 as sufficient to drive reporter gene expression in VD neurons (Howell et al., 2015) (Figure 8A). We independently confirmed this observation, and further found that the 125 bp element contains a single LIN-39 site. Mutation of this site in the context of transgenic oig-1 reporter animals (oig-1 125bp LIN-39 site MUT::tagRFP) leads to a significant reduction of tagRFP expression in VD neurons (Figure 8A–B), phenocoping the effect observed in lin-39 (n1760) null mutants (Figure 7B). We conclude that, in wild-type animals, LIN-39 acts directly, by recognizing its cognate site, to activate expression of the VD-specific gene oig-1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cis-regulatory analysis data shown in Figure 8A-B and citation to previous work (Howell et al., 2015).

claims.claim: LIN-39 and UNC-30 control oig-1 by recognizing distinct and closely spaced cis-regulatory motifs.
claims.source: Interestingly, a functional binding site for UNC-30/PITX also exists in this 125 bp element (Howell et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2017), and is spaced 11 base pairs apart from the LIN-39 site (Figure 7D), indicating that LIN-39 and UNC-30 control oig-1 by recognizing distinct and in close proximity cis-regulatory motifs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cis-regulatory analysis and citations to previous work (Howell et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2017).

claims.claim: LIN-39 acts through distinct cis-regulatory elements to activate oig-1 expression in VD versus VD-like neurons of unc-3 mutants.
claims.source: We next asked whether LIN-39 acts through the same or distinct cis-regulatory elements to drive oig-1 expression in VD versus VD-like neurons of unc-3 mutants. While oig-1 reporters in the context of a large (32.5 kb) genomic clone (fosmid) or a 2.6 kb intergenic region do show expression in both VD and VD-like neurons of unc-3 mutants, reporter animals carrying 1 kb of cis-regulatory sequence (that contains the 125 bp element) immediately upstream of ATG showed expression only in VD neurons (Figure 8A). Conversely, a distal 1.6 kb element displayed expression in VD-like cells, but no expression in VD neurons of either WT or unc-3 animals, suggesting the VD and VD-like elements are physically separated on the genome.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cis-regulatory analysis data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: Deletion of LIN-39 peak #4 in the context of a 2.6 kb oig-1 reporter results in loss of expression in VD-like cells of unc-3 mutants, whereas reporter expression is maintained in VD neurons.
claims.source: Within the 1.6 kb element, there is a LIN-39 binding peak (peak #4) based on available ChIP-Seq data on WT animals. Deletion of this peak in the context of a 2.6 kb oig-1 reporter (oig-1 2.6kb LIN-39 peak #4 DEL) resulted in loss of expression in VD-like cells of unc-3 mutants, whereas reporter expression was maintained in VD neurons (Figure 8A–B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cis-regulatory analysis data shown in Figure 8A-B.

claims.claim: The endogenous expression levels of UNC-3 are higher than LIN-39 in cholinergic motor neurons.
claims.source: Because the decrease of LIN-39 binding is accompanied by ectopic activation of VD terminal identity genes in unc-3-depleted MNs, we hypothesized that LIN-39 is the rate-limiting factor present in limited amount in cholinergic MNs. That is, in the presence of UNC-3, LIN-39 activates cholinergic MN identity genes, but in its absence LIN-39 becomes available to activate alternative identity (e.g., VD) genes. Quantification of the endogenous expression levels of both proteins indeed showed lower levels of LIN-39 expression compared to UNC-3 (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of endogenous protein levels shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: There is a gene dosage relationship between unc-3 and lin-39.
claims.source: Supporting the aforementioned hypothesis, we found a gene dosage relationship between unc-3 and lin-39. Loss of one unc-3 copy (unc-3 (n3435)/+) caused slight ectopic expression of VD genes (ser-2 in Figure 9B and flp-11 in Figure 9—figure supplement 2, panel A), but that ectopic expression is decreased by loss of one lin-39 copy (unc-3 (n3435)/+; lin-39 (n1760)/+) (Figure 9B, Figure 9—figure supplement 2, panel A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene dosage experiments shown in Figure 9B and Figure 9—figure supplement 2, panel A.

claims.claim: Knock-down of unc-3 with RNAi specifically in cholinergic motor neurons leads to ectopic expression of VD genes.
claims.source: Moreover, knock-down of unc-3 with RNAi specifically in cholinergic MNs also led to ectopic expression of VD genes (Figure 9C, Figure 9—figure supplement 2, panels B-C)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 2, panels B-C.

claims.claim: Ectopic expression of UNC-3 in VD neurons results in repression of VD gene expression.
claims.source: whereas ectopic expression of UNC-3 in VD neurons resulted in repression of VD gene expression, presumably by recruiting LIN-39 away from VD promoters (Figure 9C, Figure 9—figure supplement 2, panels B-C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by over-expression experiments shown in Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 2, panels B-C.

claims.claim: LIN-39 is sufficient to induce expression of VD terminal identity genes in cholinergic motor neurons.
claims.source: Lastly, we asked whether LIN-39 is sufficient to induce expression of VD terminal identity genes in cholinergic MNs. Indeed, we found this to be the case (Figure 9C, Figure 9—figure supplement 2, panels D-E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by over-expression experiments shown in Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 2, panels D-E.

claims.claim: 12 of the 29 mid-body locomotion features significantly affected in unc-3 single mutants are significantly suppressed in unc-3; lin-39 double mutants.
claims.source: Of the 49 mid-body features examined, 29 were significantly different in unc-3 single mutants when compared to wild-type (N2 strain) animals (see Supplementary file 3 for all 49 features). Intriguingly, 12 of these 29 features (41.37%) were significantly suppressed in unc-3; lin-39 double mutants (Figure 10A, Figure 10—figure supplement 1, panel A, Supplementary file 3)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by automated behavioral analysis data shown in Figure 10A, Figure 10—figure supplement 1, panel A, and Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: 9 of the 29 mid-body features affected in unc-3 animals are also altered in animals over-expressing lin-39 in cholinergic motor neurons.
claims.source: We found that 9 of the 29 (31.03%) mid-body features affected in unc-3 (n3435) animals were also altered in animals over-expressing lin-39 in cholinergic MNs (Figure 10B, Figure 10—figure supplement 1, panels B-C, Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by automated behavioral analysis data shown in Figure 10B, Figure 10—figure supplement 1, panels B-C, and Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: Over-expression of LIN-39 in cholinergic motor neurons leads to ectopic activation of VD, but not VC, terminal identity genes.
claims.source: First, we confirmed that in these animals expression of cholinergic MN terminal identity genes is unaffected (Figure 10—figure supplement 1, panel D). Second, we found that LIN-39 overexpression led to ectopic activation of VD, but not VC, terminal identity genes in cholinergic MNs (Figure 10—figure supplement 1, panel D)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1, panel D.

results.result: The C. elegans ventral nerve cord contains multiple motor neuron subtypes with distinct molecular identities. Five cholinergic subtypes (DA, DB, VA, VB, AS) and two GABAergic subtypes (DD, VD) control locomotion in both sexes, while sex-specific cholinergic neurons (VC in hermaphrodites, CA in males) control egg laying and mating. Each subtype is molecularly defined by combinatorial expression of terminal identity genes including ion channels, neurotransmitter receptors, and neuropeptides.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 are well-supported by citations to established literature (Von Stetina et al., 2006; White et al., 1986; Portman, 2017; Schafer, 2005; Schindelman et al., 2006) and reference to Figure 1A-B showing the anatomical organization and molecular marker expression patterns. This represents foundational background knowledge for the study.

results.result: UNC-3, the sole C. elegans ortholog of the COE transcription factor family, is selectively expressed in all sex-shared cholinergic motor neurons and directly activates a large battery of terminal identity genes. Loss of unc-3 causes striking locomotion defects, and based on its broad co-regulatory function, unc-3 has been classified as a terminal selector gene.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C8 are supported by extensive citations to prior work (Kratsios et al., 2017; Kratsios et al., 2012; Pereira et al., 2015; Prasad et al., 2008; Prasad et al., 1998; Brenner, 1974; Hobert, 2008) and reference to Figure 1B-C. This establishes the known function of UNC-3 as background for investigating its dual role.

results.result: In unc-3 mutants, approximately one-third of cholinergic motor neurons (~12 out of 39) in the mid-body ventral nerve cord region ectopically express VD-specific terminal identity markers (ser-2, oig-1) with 100% penetrance and region-specificity. These 'VD-like' neurons do not express GABA biosynthesis genes or other GABAergic markers, indicating partial rather than complete cell fate transformation.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C14 are supported by quantitative data from Figure 2A-B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, showing ectopic VD marker expression with specific cell counts (12.1 ± 2.6 neurons). The lack of GABA biosynthesis gene expression (C13) is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, panel A. The citation to Kratsios et al., 2012 (C12) supports that motor neuron numbers are normal, ruling out developmental defects.

results.result: In unc-3 mutants, a distinct population of approximately 11 cholinergic motor neurons (10.5 ± 3.7 out of 39) in the mid-body region ectopically express VC-specific terminal identity markers (ida-1, srb-16, glr-5) with 100% penetrance. These 'VC-like' neurons represent a separate population from 'VD-like' neurons, as demonstrated by non-overlapping reporter expression, and do not express acetylcholine biosynthesis genes. Markers expressed in both VD and VC neurons show additive effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C19 are supported by quantitative data from Figure 2C-D showing ectopic VC marker expression, and Figure 2E-F demonstrating no co-localization of VD and VC markers. The lack of acetylcholine biosynthesis gene expression (C17) is supported by citation to Kratsios et al., 2012. The additive effect of shared markers (C19) is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, panels D-E.

results.result: The dual role of UNC-3 extends to both C. elegans sexes. In males, loss of unc-3 results in loss of cholinergic motor neuron terminal identity features and ectopic expression of VD-specific markers in approximately 12 neurons (11.9 ± 3.9 out of 39), as well as ectopic expression of male-specific CA neuron terminal identity markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C22 are supported by quantitative data from Figure 2—figure supplement 2 showing similar phenotypes in males as observed in hermaphrodites. This demonstrates the generality of UNC-3's dual function across sexes.

results.result: UNC-3 is continuously required throughout life to prevent expression of VD and VC terminal identity features. Post-embryonic depletion of UNC-3 using auxin-inducible degradation at the L4 stage results in ectopic expression of VD and VC markers in adult motor neurons.
results.evaluation: Claim C23 is supported by data from auxin-inducible degradation experiments shown in Figure 3D-E, demonstrating that UNC-3 depletion at post-developmental stages leads to ectopic marker expression. This establishes a continuous maintenance role for UNC-3 beyond development.

results.result: UNC-3 does not act as a direct repressor of VD or VC terminal identity genes. No COE binding motifs (UNC-3's cognate binding site) are found in the cis-regulatory regions of VD or VC terminal identity genes, and UNC-3 does not prevent VD gene expression by repressing UNC-30/PITX, as demonstrated by the persistence of ectopic VD marker expression in unc-3; unc-30 double mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C25 are supported by bioinformatic analysis (Supplementary file 1) showing absence of COE motifs, and genetic data from Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing that unc-30 mutation does not suppress the unc-3 phenotype. This rules out direct repression and indirect repression via UNC-30 as mechanisms.

results.result: A forward genetic screen identified the mid-body Hox protein LIN-39 (Scr/Dfd/Hox4-5) as necessary for ectopic expression of VD and VC features in unc-3 mutants. The kas1 mutation is a splice acceptor site mutation in lin-39. LIN-39 is required for ectopic expression of VD-specific (ser-2, oig-1) and VC-specific (ida-1) genes in unc-3-depleted motor neurons, and acts cell-autonomously. Importantly, lin-39 is co-expressed with unc-3 in wild-type cholinergic motor neurons, with 28 neurons co-expressing both factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C31 are supported by data from the forward genetic screen (Figure 4A-B), Sanger sequencing identifying the kas1 mutation (Figure 4C), double mutant and RNAi experiments (Figure 4D), and co-localization analysis (Figure 4E-F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The co-expression finding (C29-C30) is critical as it contradicts the initial hypothesis of indirect repression and suggests a novel mechanism.

results.result: LIN-39 and MAB-5 act synergistically with UNC-3 to control expression of multiple cholinergic motor neuron terminal identity genes (acr-2, dbl-1, unc-77, slo-2, unc-129, del-1). Loss of lin-39 results in statistically significant decreases in expression of these genes, with effects exacerbated in lin-39; mab-5 double mutants. LIN-39 directly binds to the cis-regulatory regions of these genes, as demonstrated by ChIP-Seq data, with multiple consensus LIN-39 binding sites located within ChIP-Seq peaks. In unc-3 mutants, LIN-39 binding to these cholinergic gene loci is decreased.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 are supported by quantitative expression data (Figure 5A-B), ChIP-Seq data from modENCODE and new experiments (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and bioinformatic analysis (Supplementary file 2). The decreased LIN-39 binding in unc-3 mutants (C36) is a key finding supporting the transcriptional switch model.

results.result: LIN-39 is continuously required for ectopic activation of VD and VC terminal identity genes in unc-3 null animals. Post-embryonic auxin-mediated depletion of LIN-39 in unc-3 mutants results in statistically significant suppression of ectopic VD (ser-2), VC (glr-5), and VD/VC (flp-11) marker expression.
results.evaluation: Claim C38 is supported by data from auxin-inducible degradation experiments shown in Figure 6D-F, demonstrating that LIN-39 is continuously required for the ectopic gene expression observed in unc-3 mutants. This establishes LIN-39's ongoing role in the transcriptional switch.

results.result: LIN-39 is expressed in wild-type VD neurons at the mid-body region and is required to induce expression of VD terminal identity genes (ser-2, oig-1, flp-11). LIN-39 and UNC-30 act in parallel to activate VD terminal identity genes, as demonstrated by additive effects in double mutants. LIN-39 is continuously required to maintain VD gene expression, as shown by auxin-mediated depletion experiments. Importantly, LIN-39 loss does not affect DD-specific markers or genes expressed in both DD and VD neurons (unc-25/GAD, unc-47/VGAT), indicating selective control of VD-specific features.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C43 are supported by endogenous reporter data (Figure 7A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), expression analysis in mutants (Figure 7B), double mutant analysis (Figure 7B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, panel E), and auxin-inducible degradation experiments (Figure 7C). The selectivity for VD-specific genes (C42) is important for understanding LIN-39's precise role.

results.result: Loss of unc-30 does not lead to ectopic activation of cholinergic motor neuron terminal identity genes in GABAergic VD neurons. Expression of four cholinergic markers (acr-2, slo-1, unc-129, del-1) normally co-activated by UNC-3 and LIN-39 is unaffected in unc-30 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claim C44 is supported by data shown in Figure 7D-F demonstrating no ectopic expression of cholinergic markers in unc-30 mutants. This asymmetry (UNC-3 loss causes ectopic VD gene expression, but UNC-30 loss does not cause ectopic cholinergic gene expression) is an important finding for understanding the mechanism.

results.result: LIN-39 acts directly to activate the VD-specific gene oig-1 by recognizing its cognate binding site. A minimal 125 bp cis-regulatory element contains a single LIN-39 site, and mutation of this site significantly reduces reporter expression in VD neurons, phenocopying lin-39 null mutants. LIN-39 and UNC-30 control oig-1 by recognizing distinct cis-regulatory motifs spaced 11 base pairs apart.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46 are supported by cis-regulatory analysis data shown in Figure 8A-B, including site-directed mutagenesis experiments. The close spacing of LIN-39 and UNC-30 binding sites (C46) is supported by cis-regulatory analysis and citations to previous work (Howell et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2017).

results.result: LIN-39 acts through distinct cis-regulatory elements to activate oig-1 expression in VD versus VD-like neurons of unc-3 mutants. A proximal 1 kb element drives expression only in VD neurons, while a distal 1.6 kb element drives expression in VD-like cells but not VD neurons. Deletion of LIN-39 peak #4 within the 1.6 kb element abolishes expression in VD-like cells while maintaining VD expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48 are supported by systematic cis-regulatory analysis data shown in Figure 8A-B, demonstrating that different regulatory elements control oig-1 expression in different cell types. This is an important mechanistic finding showing how the same transcription factor can have context-dependent effects.

results.result: The endogenous expression levels of UNC-3 are higher than LIN-39 in cholinergic motor neurons, suggesting LIN-39 is a rate-limiting factor. There is a gene dosage relationship between unc-3 and lin-39: loss of one unc-3 copy causes slight ectopic VD gene expression, which is decreased by loss of one lin-39 copy. Knock-down of unc-3 with RNAi in cholinergic motor neurons leads to ectopic VD gene expression, while ectopic expression of UNC-3 in VD neurons represses VD gene expression. LIN-39 is sufficient to induce VD terminal identity gene expression in cholinergic motor neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C53 are supported by quantification of endogenous protein levels (Figure 9A), gene dosage experiments (Figure 9B, Figure 9—figure supplement 2, panel A), RNAi experiments (Figure 9C, Figure 9—figure supplement 2, panels B-C), and over-expression experiments (Figure 9C, Figure 9—figure supplement 2, panels D-E). These data collectively support the model that UNC-3 determines LIN-39's function by recruiting it to specific promoters.

results.result: Ectopic expression of VD terminal identity genes in cholinergic motor neurons is associated with locomotion defects. Of 29 mid-body locomotion features significantly affected in unc-3 mutants, 12 (41.37%) are significantly suppressed in unc-3; lin-39 double mutants. Nine of these 29 features (31.03%) are also altered in animals over-expressing lin-39 in cholinergic motor neurons, which leads to ectopic activation of VD, but not VC, terminal identity genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 are supported by automated behavioral analysis data (Figure 10A-B, Figure 10—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 3) and molecular analysis (Figure 10—figure supplement 1, panel D). The behavioral data provide functional validation that the molecular changes observed have physiological consequences. However, the correlation between molecular and behavioral phenotypes, while suggestive, does not definitively prove causation.
